speaker_role: student (recent applicant sharing personal experience with alumni interviews, not a counselor or admissions officer)
key_insights: Distinguishes 'informational' interviews (student-led, meant to inform the student about the school, not evaluative) from 'evaluative' interviews (interviewer assesses the applicant's character/fit)
States interview weight varies significantly by school, and argues that at the most selective schools alumni interviews carry relatively little weight in the final admissions decision
Notes interview length varies widely (his own ranged from ~20 minutes to 2 hours) and reports no correlation in his own experience between interview length and admission outcome
Recommends business-casual attire rather than formal wear, framing the interview as closer to a normal conversation than a high-stakes evaluation
Suggests practicing with a mock interviewer for common questions (tell me about yourself, why this school, why this major, extracurriculars) while still preparing to think on the spot for follow-ups
Argues that not receiving an interview offer doesn't indicate anything negative, since interview availability often just depends on whether an alumni interviewer is available in the applicant's area
States that on balance a bad interview can hurt an application and a great one can help, but an average interview likely has little to no effect on the outcome
specific_numbers_or_facts: Speaker reports his own interview at Penn lasted about 20 minutes (resulted in a waitlist) and his MIT interview lasted about 2 hours (resulted in a rejection), used anecdotally to argue interview length doesn't predict outcome
notable_or_distinctive: The claim that his longest interview (2 hours, MIT) resulted in rejection while his shortest (20 minutes, Penn) resulted in a waitlist is a distinctive personal anecdote used to argue against assuming interview length signals anything about admission chances.
reliability_notes: Entirely based on one student's personal anecdotal experience at a handful of schools; generalizations about how much interviews 'really' matter across schools are the speaker's own inference, not sourced from admissions offices.
